tagline: A great poem about an innocent man who loses everything, argues with his friends and with God, and meets God in the storm.
overview:
Job is the Bible's longest and most searching treatment of innocent suffering. A short prose story frames it: Job, a wealthy and godly man from the land of Uz, loses his flocks, his servants, his ten children, and finally his health, because God has allowed the accuser to test whether Job's devotion is real or merely paid for. The reader is told this from the start. Job never is.

Between the prose opening and the prose ending lies a long poem. Job curses the day he was born. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, come to comfort him and end up arguing that suffering like his must be punishment for sin, so he should repent. Job refuses to confess what he hasn't done, and he turns from them to God, demanding a hearing. A younger man, Elihu, adds four speeches of his own. Then the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, not with an explanation of the test but with a tour of creation, from the foundations of the earth to the wild animals and the great beasts Behemoth and Leviathan. Job falls silent, retracts his words, and the story closes with God rebuking the friends, saying that Job has spoken rightly of him, and restoring Job's fortunes.

The book matters because it refuses the easy answers. It denies that all suffering is deserved, it lets a righteous man protest to God at length and in the Bible's own pages, and it ends not with a theory of evil but with an encounter. Generations of readers, believers and unbelievers alike, have found in it the most honest words ever written about pain.
author: The book doesn't name its author, and no other part of the Bible says who wrote it. A Jewish tradition recorded in the Babylonian Talmud credits Moses, which fits the book's patriarchal feel: Job offers sacrifices himself as head of his family, measures wealth in flocks and herds, and lives 140 years after his restoration. Most modern scholars, conservative and critical alike, think the author was an unnamed Israelite poet of great learning, writing in a Hebrew rich with rare words and with many Aramaic features, and drawing on a story about Job that may have been older than the poem. Some critical scholars also think the book grew in stages, with the Elihu speeches (chapters 32 to 37) and the poem on wisdom (chapter 28) added later, while others argue that the book as it stands shows a single design. What is clear is that the writer knew the wisdom traditions of Israel and its neighbors and wrote the most demanding poetry in the Old Testament.
date: There are two questions: when Job lived and when the book was written. The story is set in a world like that of the patriarchs, with no mention of Israel, the exodus, the law of Moses, the temple, or the kings, and Ezekiel mentions Job alongside Noah and Daniel as a famous righteous man of old (Ezekiel 14:14, 20). The writing of the book is harder to fix. Proposals range from the time of Solomon (tenth century BC), when Israel's wisdom writing flourished, through the seventh century, to the period after the Babylonian exile (sixth to fourth centuries BC), a view often argued from the book's language and its reflection on undeserved suffering. Copies and fragments of Job, including an Aramaic translation, were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, so the book was complete and in use well before the time of Jesus. The honest answer is that the date of writing is unknown and the positions are held by capable scholars on each side.
setting:
Job lives in Uz, a land east of Israel whose exact location is uncertain. Lamentations 4:21 links Uz with Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea, and some scholars look instead to the regions north and east toward Aram. The friends come from places with Edomite and Arabian associations: Eliphaz is a Temanite, and Teman was an Edomite clan descended from Esau (Genesis 36:11); Bildad is a Shuhite, and Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Job himself is not an Israelite. The raiders who strike his household, the Sabeans and Chaldeans, are desert and border peoples, and the caravans of Tema and Sheba (6:19) belong to the Arabian trade routes.

The wider world of the book is the ancient Near East, where wise men in several cultures wrestled with suffering. Babylonian texts such as the poem often called Ludlul bel nemeqi, in which a devout man describes his affliction and eventual restoration by the god Marduk, and the so-called Babylonian Theodicy, a dialogue between a sufferer and a friend, show that Job's question was not Israel's alone. Job differs from them in its length, its daring, and above all in the God who finally speaks.
purpose: Job was written to test and deepen the wisdom tradition, not to overturn it. Books like Proverbs teach that the righteous generally flourish and the wicked generally fall, which is true as a pattern of God's world. Job asks what happens when the pattern breaks, and it shows what goes wrong when the pattern is turned into a rule that can be run backward: if you are suffering, you must have sinned. The book also asks the question the accuser raises in chapter 1, whether anyone serves God for nothing, and answers it through Job's clinging, protesting faith. For its first readers, and for every reader since, it gives permission to bring grief and complaint straight to God, and it warns comforters against speaking for God more confidently than they know.
story: Job belongs to the Bible's wisdom books, alongside Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, with the Psalms and the Song of Songs close by. It stands somewhat apart from the main storyline that runs from Abraham through Israel's history, since Job is not an Israelite and the covenant with Israel is never mentioned. That is part of its point: the questions it asks belong to every human being under the one creator. Within the whole story, Job stands between the good creation of Genesis, which the LORD's speeches revisit, and the long record of Israel's own suffering in exile, where the question of whether God is just to his people became urgent. The New Testament cites Job's perseverance and the Lord's compassion toward him (James 5:11).
christ: The book does not predict Jesus, and its greatest lines should not be forced into prophecy. But it opens questions that the rest of the Bible answers in Christ. Job longs for a mediator who could stand between him and God (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19), and a redeemer who lives (19:25); Christians hear in these longings the shape of what God gives in Jesus, the one mediator who is both God and man. Job is an innocent sufferer whom his friends count as a sinner; Jesus is the fully innocent one who was numbered with the transgressors and cried out to God in the words of Psalm 22. The accuser who questions Job's heart before God is the same enemy the New Testament says Christ has defeated. And where Job's restoration comes at the end of his story, the resurrection of Jesus is the pledge that God's final word over the suffering of the righteous is life.
reading: Read Job as poetry and as drama, not as a set of proof texts. Much of what is said in the book is said by characters the LORD later corrects (42:7), so a verse from Eliphaz, Bildad, or Zophar isn't automatically the book's teaching, even when it sounds pious; watch who is speaking. Read the prologue carefully, because the reader knows what Job doesn't, and that gap drives the whole book. Expect repetition across the three cycles of speeches, and watch how the friends harden and how Job's thought moves. The Hebrew is often obscure, and translations differ more here than almost anywhere else in the Old Testament. Common misreadings include treating the heavenly scene as a full explanation of all suffering, treating the friends as simply wicked (they say many true things and apply them wrongly), and treating the happy ending as a reward that makes the losses not matter.

structure.title: Prologue: the test in heaven and on earth
structure.summary: A prose story introduces Job, the scenes in the heavenly court, the loss of his wealth, children, and health, and the arrival of his three friends.

structure.title: Job's lament
structure.summary: Job breaks a seven-day silence by cursing the day of his birth and asking why the miserable are given life.

structure.title: The first cycle of speeches
structure.summary: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar each speak, and Job answers each one; the friends urge repentance and Job protests his innocence and appeals to God.

structure.title: The second cycle
structure.summary: The friends dwell on the fate of the wicked, and Job, deserted by everyone, reaches toward a witness and a redeemer.

structure.title: The third cycle
structure.summary: Eliphaz accuses Job of specific sins, Bildad gives a short speech, Zophar does not speak, and the debate breaks down.

structure.title: A poem on wisdom
structure.summary: People can mine the earth for treasure but cannot find wisdom; God alone knows its place, and the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

structure.title: Job's final defense
structure.summary: Job remembers his former honor, laments his present shame, and swears a series of oaths of innocence, calling on God to answer.

structure.title: The speeches of Elihu
structure.summary: A younger man, angry at Job and at the friends, argues that God speaks through suffering to warn and to save.

structure.title: The LORD speaks from the whirlwind
structure.summary: God questions Job about creation and its wild creatures, and Job responds in humility and repentance.

structure.title: Epilogue
structure.summary: The LORD rebukes the friends, accepts Job's prayer for them, and restores Job's household and fortunes.

themes.title: Innocent suffering
themes.body: The book's starting point is a man whom God himself calls blameless and upright, and who suffers not because of his sin but because of his righteousness. That fact, given to the reader in chapters 1 and 2, overturns any simple equation of suffering with guilt. The book does not say that no suffering is deserved; it says that not all of it is, and that people who assume otherwise will speak falsely about God.

themes.title: Disinterested faith
themes.body: The accuser's question, whether Job fears God for nothing, is the book's hidden hinge. If faith is only a transaction, it will collapse when the payments stop. Job's losses test whether a human being can love God for God's own sake. His faith is not calm; it protests, accuses, and demands. But it never lets go of God, and the book presents that stubborn holding on as what faith looks like under the weight of loss.

themes.title: The failure of the comforters
themes.body: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar arrive in love and sit with Job in silence for seven days, which is the best thing they do. Once they begin speaking they defend a theology in which God always rewards the good and punishes the wicked in this life, and they apply it to a man they don't understand. In the end God says they have not spoken rightly about him. The book warns every counselor, pastor, and friend against true general principles misapplied to a particular person.

themes.title: Lament and honest speech to God
themes.body: Job curses his birthday, accuses God of treating him as an enemy, and demands a trial. Yet God says at the end that Job, unlike his friends, has spoken what is right. The book shows that complaint addressed to God can be an act of faith, belonging with the lament psalms, and that God would rather hear anguish spoken to him than tidy doctrine spoken about him.

themes.title: God's wisdom in creation
themes.body: The LORD's speeches do not explain the heavenly test. Instead they show Job a world far larger and wilder than any human account of it, full of creatures that serve no human purpose and are still under God's care. The effect is to set Job's suffering inside the wisdom and freedom of the creator, and to move Job from hearing about God to seeing him (42:5).

keyChapters.why: The heavenly scene and the first test introduce the accuser's question and Job's great confession of worship in loss.
Job's lament sets the tone for the poem, bringing raw grief into the open before any argument begins.
Abandoned by friends and family, Job declares that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God.
A poem on the search for wisdom, which only God possesses, and which begins in the fear of the Lord.
Job's final oaths of innocence give a portrait of Old Testament righteousness in private and public life.
The LORD answers from the whirlwind, questioning Job about the foundations of the world.
Job's response, the rebuke of the friends, and the restoration of Job's household bring the book to its close.
